title: FEMA workforce reductions can narrow disaster-assistance capacity before survivor outcomes are visible
source_unit: GAO-26-108427 review of FEMA workforce size, composition, planning, deployment, and mission readiness
geography: United States; FEMA headquarters, 10 regions, incident-management cadres, and disaster-response workforce

observations.period: Fiscal year 2025 through April 18, 2026; report published August 4, 2026

denominator.unit: average FEMA employees in fiscal year 2025; workforce and separation measures use separate agency-defined universes

separations.value: More than 4,300 employees separated from FEMA in fiscal year 2025, a 55% increase from fiscal year 2024

current_workforce.unit: FEMA personnel reported employed as of April 18, 2026

planning_status.value: FEMA rescinded its strategic plan and did not base 2025-2026 workforce reductions and proposed actions on a workforce analysis, according to GAO

institutional_knowledge.value: FEMA officials told GAO that separations resulted in lost institutional knowledge and exacerbated longstanding workforce challenges

observations.method: GAO analyzed FEMA workforce size and composition, workforce and policy documents, executive-branch actions, and interviews with FEMA headquarters officials and officials in all 10 regions; it evaluated workforce planning against key practices.
observations.uncertainty: The review establishes staffing and planning conditions and reported operational consequences, not a causal estimate of survivor-level denial, wait time, housing loss, recovery, or health. Workforce counts use different dates and agency-defined categories; FEMA may augment permanent staff with temporary and surge personnel.
observations.subgroup: FEMA permanent, CORE, reservist, local-hire, and surge personnel; incident-management cadres; headquarters and regional staff; concurrent-disaster teams; survivors relying on Individual Assistance, grants, information, and recovery programs.
observations.counterinterpretation: Workforce reductions can coexist with temporary surge, local hiring, cross-agency augmentation, process changes, and future strategic planning. Staffing capacity alone does not prove that a particular survivor experienced delay or that more staff would have produced a better outcome.

denominator.unit: GAO-reviewed FEMA concurrent-disaster and surge-capacity case

concurrent_deployment.unit: FEMA employees deployed for Hurricanes Helene and Milton according to FEMA officials

post_deployment_availability.unit: percent of FEMA incident-management workforce available to deploy in November 2024 after the two hurricanes

surge_support.value: FEMA officials anticipated about 240 DHS Surge Capacity Force employees available for 2026 hurricane-season support, down from 600 in 2025

service_link.value: GAO reports that Texas flood survivors experienced long wait times and unanswered calls after FEMA reduced surge-support resources and call-center staffing

observations.method: GAO synthesis of FEMA data, agency documentation, official interviews, and prior GAO disaster-assistance reviews.
observations.uncertainty: The cases show a plausible capacity-to-access route but do not provide a representative survivor-level contact-failure rate, causal counterfactual, or downstream housing and income effect.
observations.subgroup: Residents of concurrent or large disasters, FEMA Individual Assistance applicants, call-center users, incident-management personnel, and regions requiring cross-region deployment.
observations.counterinterpretation: High deployment can reflect extraordinary demand rather than a staffing failure, and unanswered calls may also reflect call volume, communication systems, or application complexity. The evidence does not isolate one cause.

related_sources.claim: Related GAO review reports FEMA assistance scale alongside survivor communication and post-disaster housing challenges.
Related GAO review examines disaster-assistance scams and the information environment facing survivors.

boundary: This record adds a federal disaster-workforce and assistance-delivery capacity pathway. It does not establish a survivor-level causal wait-time, denial, housing, income, health, trust, or political-action effect, and it does not show that workforce reductions alone caused any individual outcome.
